title: What happened to request 102?

beats.say: Yesterday the scorer read these three requests. Two answers matched. Today the same scorer reports a perfect score. The model still has the very same answers on file. What could have changed?

Slide request one hundred two out of the file. Two matches remain among the two requests read. Put the request back and open its saved fields. The expected label is blocked. The prediction is escalated, in capitals, with a space at each end. What will Python record when it compares those labels?

title: Follow line two into Python

beats.say: The file gives us a line of text. The call to json dot loads decodes it into a Python dictionary. The equals sign binds that object to row. A dictionary lets you look up a value by name. The brackets around prediction take us straight to the saved label.

Keep an eye on the saved field while we normalize its value under a new name. Strip removes the spaces at its two ends. Lower then changes the capitals to lowercase. These methods return strings. The capitals are still there in the dictionary. We apply both methods to the expected label too.

Read the two normalized words. Double equals compares them. A single equals sign binds the result to a name. The comparison returns False. That value adds zero to the match count. Where does it go in the list of decisions?

title: Where does False go?

beats.say: Start with an empty list of decisions. On each visit, row refers to one dictionary. Python runs the indented body before moving on. The first pair matches. Append True. The second differs. Append False. The third matches. Append True for the last request. Look straight down from request one hundred two.

Adding those Booleans counts each True as one and False as zero, giving two matches. Len counts all three Booleans. The middle request takes up a place just like its neighbors. Divide the counts to get two thirds. Python prints the fraction to three decimal places. We'll need the two integers again.

title: What did Python receive?

beats.say: Look at the pieces we just used. A dictionary lets us ask for a named field. A list keeps the rows in visit order. A tuple lets a function return the matches, total and fraction together.
The label is text, the counts are integers, division gives a float and each comparison gives a Boolean. None expresses an absent value.

Read the three sevens. The quotes are part of the evidence. The integer and float compare equal numerically, while text seven does not. Use a key to read a dictionary field and an index to read a position in a list.

Bind the local name prediction to the saved string. Now bind that name to seven. Look up the field again. The dictionary still holds the string with capitals and spaces. Assignment changed which value the local name refers to.
Suppose the producer wrote the number seven where it promised a label. We could call str on it. Turning a numeric prediction into text seven would hide a producer error inside a mismatch.

Convert with int, float or str only when that conversion makes sense for the field. Our text rule has limits too. Strip leaves the space inside block ed. Two different explanations with the same meaning can also fail exact match.

title: Which edit reaches the baseline?

beats.say: Start a fresh row with the two normalized labels from request one hundred two. The expected label is blocked and the prediction is escalated. Give the baseline list a second name, trial. Follow both arrows before you edit. Now set the trial prediction to blocked.
Start at the name baseline and follow slot zero to the row. Its prediction now reads blocked. You made one assignment through trial. Reading through either name takes you to that same changed field.

Reset to escalated and copy the outer list. You can see two lists now. Follow slot zero in either one. Run the same mutation through trial. Both arrows still end at the same dictionary, so baseline reads blocked again.

Reset again. This comprehension copies each row into a new list. Now mutate the copied row. This time the baseline keeps escalated. Every value in this row is a string. What if one field held a list we could append to?

title: Where does the tag land?

beats.say: Give the row one more field, an empty list of tags. Copying each row gives two dictionaries, but both dictionaries initially refer to the same tags list. Trace the two arrows to their tips. If we append a tag through trial, where will baseline look for it?

First set the trial prediction to blocked. That assignment changes only the copied dictionary, so the baseline keeps escalated. Now append the tag review through trial. Both arrows still point to the list where the tag landed. That's how baseline can read a word we added through trial.

Replay from the original row with an empty list. Copy the row and give trial its own copy of the tags list. Follow the two arrows now. Append review through trial. Only trial sees it. A shallow copy separates one container at a time.
Our scorer can leave the rows alone and build a separate list of decisions. If you need to filter rows, collect the ones you want in a new list as you go.

title: What does the caller get back?

beats.say: Let's give those two string operations a home. In exact match, the parameters name the expected label and the prediction. The indented body normalizes both. Return sends the comparison back to the loop. For blocked and escalated the return value is False.

Try a different caller. It supplies approved and a prediction in capitals with spaces around it. The function returns True after normalization. The string and Boolean hints tell a reader or a static checker what values the function expects and returns. What would happen if the caller passed seven?

Pass seven as the prediction. Python binds that integer to the parameter despite the string hint. At the lookup for strip, it raises AttributeError. A hint helps a reader or a static checker. An explicit field check while loading can also tell the producer which line to repair.

title: Run the scorer from the checkout

beats.say: Let's run that function on a copy of the Docker lab file. In the lab, request one hundred two says escalated in lowercase. Our copy uses capitals and a space at each end. Start in the project directory.

The project file declares the supported Python versions. Our checkout pin selects the three twelve family used in the Docker lab. Run uv sync. It builds the project environment and, on this first setup, writes the dependency lock.

Use uv run to launch the scorer in that environment. Path builds a path relative to the project directory we're standing in. Open the file as UTF eight and the loop visits one line at a time. The handle gives Python text. Each nonblank line here contains one JSON object.

title: Rebuild the scorer on another machine

beats.say: The project accepts Python three twelve and newer. Our checkout pins three twelve. Look at the two patch releases in the middle. Both fit that pin. Three thirteen fits only the project range. Each checkout keeps its installed packages in its own virtual environment.

On a new project, uv init with the bare option creates the project declaration. Python pin writes dot-python-version. Sync creates the local environment and dependency lock. Uv run uses the project environment without activating a shell. Activation changes which executable the shell finds.
Python's built-in venv can also isolate a project. Keep the Docker lab's requirements file for the image build.

Send your colleague the project file, the pin and the lock. Commit those portable inputs in Git. Their machine builds its own environment. Suppose someone adds a dependency to the project declaration alone. A locked sync or run stops before executing the scorer. The stale lock stays as it was.
Plain uv run can update it. Even a clean install leaves one question open. Which rows did the command read?

title: From a function call to a printed score

beats.say: Inside score examples, matches starts at zero. For each row, if tests the Boolean. On the first visit, add one. On the middle visit, skip the indented addition. On the last visit, add one again. The loop still visited three rows. The total comes from the length of that list.
The function returns matches, total and their fraction together. The caller unpacks that tuple into three names.

A test imports the same function that the command runs. The name equals main guard decides which happens. Direct execution selects main. An import makes the functions available without scoring a file. In the command arguments, the first entry names the script.
With one extra argument, use the path in slot one. With just the script name, use the default file. Try two extra arguments. The wrapper exits with usage instructions before opening either path.

Watch the order in main. The loader must return before the scorer counts anything. If the score falls below the floor, the command has already printed the metric. It sends the failure message to standard error and exits with status one.
An input exception can instead stop before any metric is printed. Let's try breaking one field.

title: Where does line two stop?

beats.say: Yesterday's row made it all the way to a comparison. In a copy of the file, replace the prediction with a bare seven. Look at the quotes on the line above. Seven is legal JSON too. Decoding produces a dictionary with an integer value. Will that seven ever reach the comparison?

Now look at the field check. Each of the three required fields must be a string with at least one character left after stripping whitespace. Python found the field. Its value is an integer, so the type check tells Python to raise TypeError.
Read the exception aloud. Line two, prediction must be a string. The loader cannot return its list. Even the good row above line two produces no printed score on this run.

Keep the rest of the line and erase the seven. The closing brace comes immediately after the colon. This time the line fails inside json dot loads. The loader adds line two to that error. Look across the three versions.
The original gives the scorer two text labels to compare. The middle line tells us someone saved a seven. On the last line, decoding stopped before we even had a field to check.

title: What survives decoding?

beats.say: Look at what the decoder hands to Python. Objects become dictionaries. Arrays become lists. True becomes a Boolean and null becomes None. Seven becomes an integer. A decimal point or an exponent gives us a float. There's a limit on reading long decimal integers.

With Python three twelve's default limit, one digit past forty-three hundred raises ValueError during decoding. This loader catches JSONDecodeError, so it doesn't add a line number to that digit-limit error. Now try the empty array as a whole record. It decodes to a list.
Our parser requires a dictionary and raises TypeError.

In this copy of the file, the same line names prediction twice. Follow the reader from left to right. There's just one slot for that key. First it holds blocked. Then the decoder reads the same key again. Only escalated survives in the dictionary.

The loader copies prompt, expected and prediction into the checked row. Extra fields stay behind. Compare the surviving prediction with blocked. The comparison returns False. Could you recover the earlier word by inspecting this dictionary?

Go back to the raw line. Give the decoder our function through the object pairs hook option. Now the function sees each pair in file order. It saves the first prediction key. Advance one pair. The name under the reader matches the saved name. Our hook stops here, before the decoder returns a dictionary.

This row has two expected labels, hold and sent. The prediction is sent. The scorer ignores the extra confidence flag. Make a copy and remove the first expected field. Which row will the strict hook pass to the scorer?

The default decoder keeps the last expected label. Trim the spaces and lowercase the letters. Both rows compare sent with sent. Both score True. Now follow the strict hook. In the saved row it stops at the second expected key.
In the edited row each key occurs once. That row reaches the scorer and scores True.

title: Which line number belongs in the error?

beats.say: Open a fresh handle on this four-line file as UTF eight. Enumerate starts at one. The loop skips a blank, accepts a request, then skips another blank. The next object lacks prediction. If you were fixing the file in an editor, which line would you open?
Report the missing prediction on physical line four. That's where someone opening the file will find it.

Try reading all four raw lines. After the first loop reaches end of file, a second loop over that handle has no remaining lines. Now insert an empty array above the broken request. Opening a new handle starts another traversal. This time, parse each nonblank line.
Keep your finger on the physical line numbers. The inserted brackets are valid JSON. Which check stops the loader first? Does the accepted row produce a score?
On physical line four, the brackets decode to an empty list. The object check raises TypeError on line four. The loader accepted just one row, on line two. The request on line five is still unread.
The with block closes the file as the exception travels back to main. Main prints no metric because the loader never returned the rows.

Back on the valid file, this loader appends every accepted dictionary to a list. It reads the source a line at a time, but those dictionaries stay in memory after the file closes. The returned list can be visited again.
For a much larger file you could keep just running counts. You'd still need to decide what to do if a later line fails.

title: Which requests can the score speak for?

beats.say: Before Python can open that file, it has to compile our program. Look at the if statement. Its missing colon raises SyntaxError during parsing. Python can also raise SyntaxError later in compilation, before this module runs. With valid code, FileNotFoundError can occur later when opening the input.

Bad JSON is later still. The loader catches JSONDecodeError and raises a ValueError with the line number. The explicit from-error cause preserves the original decoding failure beneath that added context.

Once Python has a dictionary, look at the field. A missing key raises KeyError. A seven in the prediction field raises TypeError. A string of spaces raises ValueError. If two valid labels still differ after stripping and lowercasing, the comparison returns False.
To locate a failure, read the last exception and its message, then follow the calls upward. Catch it where you can add context, recover, or give the command an intentional exit.

Our loader stops on the first invalid nonblank line. Suppose a different loader keeps going. It saves every rejected request and its reason in a quarantine file. Watch these four requests come through. Record attempted, accepted and rejected counts, reasons and identities.

For release, the scorer has to get at least two thirds of its comparisons right. At least ninety-five percent of incoming requests have to reach that comparison. Use the IDs in the two paths. Which requests go in each denominator? Would you release this run?

Two of the three accepted labels match. That's enough for accuracy. Only three of the four attempted requests were accepted. Seventy-five percent falls short of the required ninety-five. Hold this release. The quarantine record identifies request one hundred four and the seven in its prediction field.
Compare that with the producer's record for the same request. If the producer recorded a text label, trace how that label became a number on its way into the file.

title: Can this value be a probability?

beats.say: The scorer ignores extra fields. Suppose a future version reads confidence as a probability. Feed its proposed validator the JSON value true. In Python, Boolean is a subclass of integer. True passes an integer check and behaves like one in numeric operations. Accepting it here would turn a yes into a probability of one.

The helper rejects a Boolean or a value outside int and float first. Next it checks the interval from zero through one, then converts to float and checks that the result is finite. Zero and point seven five pass.
The quoted version stopped at the first check because the decoder returned a string. The range check rejects NaN, infinity and decoded numbers outside the interval.

Look at the three highlighted values. One is NaN and two are positive infinity. All three are nonfinite floats. Python's default JSON decoder accepts nonstandard NaN and Infinity. Even valid JSON one-e-four-hundred overflows this float path to infinity. The interval check catches all three.
It also rejects an enormous integer before float conversion can overflow. For a field permitted to exceed one, keep an explicit finite check if infinity would make the value unusable.

Compare these two decimal spellings near one. The final digit differs. As an exact decimal, the second value is above the allowed interval. Decode them as ordinary Python floats. Both round to one. Both pass the check on the decoded value.
To distinguish decimals this close to one, you'd need to preserve their precision when you read them.

title: Do both printed scores clear the floor?

beats.say: Remember our printed two thirds? A float stores a binary approximation. Formatting it to three places gives the text on the report. Here are two runs with nine thousand scored requests apiece. Both print zero point six six seven. To apply a floor of two thirds, what evidence is missing from these reports?

Unfold the counts. A has five thousand nine hundred ninety-nine matches. B has six thousand. Each tick on the scale stands for one match. Compare three times each match count with twice the total. Which run reaches the two-thirds floor?

Place A on the scale. Three times its matches is seventeen thousand nine hundred ninety-seven, just below eighteen thousand. Now mark B. It has one more match. Both sides equal eighteen thousand, so B passes. The report rounded away that difference. Math dot is close is useful when your contract allows a tolerance. This release rule uses an exact count.

Here's why the same trick works for any fraction a over b, with a positive denominator and a nonempty run. Multiply both sides by b times total. Both factors are positive, so the inequality points the same way. Compare b times matches with a times total.

For this scorer that gives three times matches at least two times total. Matches must be between zero and the number of rows, and there has to be at least one row. An empty list would give zero on both sides and pass the bare comparison.
The scorer rejects that empty list before dividing.

title: Did the parser reject the right thing?

beats.say: How do we keep this behavior when somebody edits the scorer? Pytest discovers our test functions and runs their assertions. The same parser test tries each of five supplied non-string predictions, including a Boolean and null. Pytest collects ten cases in total.
A test that asks for the temporary path fixture gets its own directory. We can put blank lines in a test file without touching the scored requests.

Look at the little block around the parser call. Pytest expects that call to raise the named exception type or a subclass. Returning a row fails. Raising a different type fails too. The match argument searches the message for a pattern. The caret anchors the start.
Read the character after the two. The colon makes line twenty fail and line two pass. Both calls raised TypeError, but only one sent us to the right line.

Run the tests on a disposable copy. Now remove just the string type check. Python tries to strip values like seven and raises a different exception. Those five rejection tests fail. Put the check back and all ten pass again.

Read the setup of the count test. It passes three dictionaries written inside the test. Deleting a line from the file on disk never changes those dictionaries. How would you exercise the file the command actually scores?

title: Open the two perfect reports

beats.say: Bring back the three requests. Two of the three predictions match. Our floor compares six with six, so the run passes. Suppose a report tomorrow says one hundred percent. What would establish that the model corrected the middle answer?

Here are two such reports. They used the same scorer and the same lock. In one run the model supplied a new answer for the middle request. In the other run someone removed a row. The strips at the top show just the percentages.
Which run corrected request one hundred two? Both percentages are one hundred. Name the evidence you would ask to see before choosing.
Open both strips and line up the IDs. In run A the middle column holds blocked. All three requests match. In run B the slot for one hundred two is empty. Two out of two.

The original count test still scores its three local dictionaries. To check the file that B used, change where the test gets its rows. Load that path with load examples. Score the returned rows. Compare those counts with the baseline of two matches in three rows. The assertion fails. B supplied two matches in only two rows.
The match count held steady while the total fell. Open the input diff. That minus sign identifies the request B dropped. Restore the line before you compare models on this fixture.

title: Would the same command run on a clean machine?

beats.say: The dependency lock answers a different question. With uv run, an extra installed package can remain in the current environment. Uv sync, by default, removes packages that are not selected. Adding locked to a command makes it check that the lock agrees with the project. The choice between run and sync still matters.

Begin with a disposable environment and manually install the undeclared package six. The first locked run can import it. Now run locked sync. It removes the extra installation. Try the same import again. Python raises ModuleNotFoundError.

If your program needs this helper, declare it, then review the change to the lock. A copy made before the sync would include that helper's files. On the other machine, rebuild the environment from the project files.

Replay the command from a clean checkout or sync the environment first. Keep the code, input file and command with the interpreter pin and dependency records. Our scorer has no randomness. When a later program draws random values, record which generator it uses and its seed.
Hardware and library differences can still change the result. Let's try the scorer once more, with a file we haven't seen.

title: What will this file print?

beats.say: This file starts with a blank line. Watch the loader take the next four requests. On the last line the expected label is in quotes. Look at the prediction beside it. When you run this file, what reaches standard output?

JSON true decodes successfully to a Boolean. The parser asks for a string. On physical line six it raises TypeError. Look at those four IDs the loader already had. The function stopped before it could return that list. Main prints no metric. Where would you look to find out what the model actually said?

Open the producer's log for that same request. The saved label was the text open. Restore that word to the file. The expected label stays blocked. Start again and load all five requests. Now the scorer can compare the labels in order.

Read from left to right. Each position belongs to one request. Count the True values and then count the positions. With the floor still at two thirds, what score will print, and will the command pass?

Follow the five decisions back to the request IDs. Each False still takes a place. Three matches out of five. That score goes to standard output. For the floor, triple the matches and double the total. Nine is one short of ten. The two-thirds gate fails.

Read the two output streams in order. Standard output has the score. Standard error has the failed gate, and the command exits with status one. Compare that with the first run, which stopped in the loader. Which two valid requests explain the misses on this run?

Follow each False back to its request. Five hundred two and five hundred five both had usable labels, and both comparisons failed. You can take those two records back to the model team. These decisions could form an array with one entry per request.

Keep a finger on the second and fifth positions as the decisions become an array. Each position still belongs to the same request. In the NumPy lesson, we'll track the word that belongs to each row before we combine or reduce an array.
